OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $h(x)$ count the number of integers $1\leq a<b<x$ such that $(a,b)=1$ and $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)$, where $\sigma$ is the sum of divisors function.
Is it true that $h(x)>x^{2-o(1)}$?
#824: [Er59c,p.172][Er74b,p.202]
number theory
Erdős [Er74b] proved that $\limsup h(x)/x= \infty$, and claimed a similar proof for this problem. A complete proof that $h(x)/x\to \infty$ was provided by Pollack and Pomerance [PoPo16].
A similar question can be asked if we replace the condition $(a,b)=1$ with the condition that $a$ and $b$ are squarefree. Weisenberg suggests another variant, with the condition that there are no proper factors $u\mid a$ and $v\mid b$ such that $\sigma(u)=\sigma(v)$ and $(u,a/u)=(v,b/v)=1$, which is the weakest restriction one can impose that is still strong enough to eliminate trivial duplicates.
Additional thanks to: Desmond Weisenberg

 One find the values of $\sigma(n)$ in https://oeis.org/A000203/b000203.txt.
(there are 31525 many different values here, and the maximum multiplicity is 183, i.e. there is no $n$ for which there are more than $183$ different values $a$ with $\sigma(a)=n$)
Related to the accompanying text below the question:
"and claimed a similar proof for this problem."
It is not for the problem, but it is a similar proof for the lim version instead of limsup version
(https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1974-27.pdf, page 202)

 [PoPo16] closely ties this problem to that of locating many primes which are one less than a smooth number (one uses products of such primes to create lots of collisions $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)$). In particular, if for any fixed $\theta>1$ and large $y$ it can be shown that there are $\gg y^{\theta-o(1)}$ primes $p \leq y^\theta$ with $p+1$ $y$-rough, then the arguments in that paper give a positive answer to this question. (This type of result is known for $\theta \approx 3.377$, giving rise to a lower bound roughly of the form $h(x) \gg x^{1.4}$.)

A partial proof 
claimed by Cam (using GPT 5.6 high).
 Summary:
 The main point of this proof is to establish that the known exponent can be improved to \(\frac{13}{8}\). Using Pascadi's \(5/8\) exponent of distribution, we construct many primes \(p\) for which \(p+1=md\), with \(d\) highly structured and smooth. A counting argument using Cauchy--Schwarz, followed by removal of common prime factors and control of the resulting multiplicities, yields our improved exponent.
AI Disclosure: AI was used for the core idea of the proof, for locating relevant literature (notably Pascadi's theorem), and for much of the writeup. All AI-generated material was reviewed by a human before submission.
